#7794. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.

#7792. Former Cravath employee considers plea deal after insider trading charges

A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal. (Image from Shutterstock)

A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal.

Federal prosecutors in New York allege that Chetram Balli, who is also known as Tony Balli, 54, accessed nonpublic information through his role as a document processing specialist for Cravath and traded ahead of at least five of the law firm’s major deals.

According to Law360, a one-page form order signed Thursday by U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcia M. Henry of the Eastern District of New York reveals that federal prosecutors and Balli are engaged in plea discussions.

The order also shows that Balli’s defense counsel requested more time to focus on negotiations without the risk of not being adequately prepared for a trial, Law360 reports.

Law360 requested but did not receive comment from either party.

Balli began working for Cravath in 1989. According to prosecutors, he supported attorneys by producing legal documents and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings and at times had access to confidential information.

Balli was arrested Thursday after prosecutors filed a criminal complaint against him and alleged that he made more than $70,000 in illicit profits.

#7788. Three Iranian-Backed Operatives Indicted for Their Roles in Nearly 20 Terrorist Attacks and Attempted Attacks Across Europe and the United States

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

“Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”

“This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”

“Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests.  My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”

According to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of New York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

Al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York. The picture below shows al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

As alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

On or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

On or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”

In September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

While in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

For example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”

On or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

The Justice Department praised the outstanding investigative work of the FBI’s New York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, and the FBI Washington Field Office, Counterterrorism Division, as well as the assistance of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the NYPD, the New York State Police, and the Department of State.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey W. Coyle, Sarah L. Kushner, David J. Robles, and Chelsea L. Scism for the Southern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with assistance from James Donnelly and Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

A superseding indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7787. Eleven new relists in search of four votes

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

First, some old business. The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser. After three relists, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown finally got the nod. The court will decide when bankruptcy courts can refuse to enforce arbitration agreements in suits alleging violations of the automatic stay. But two-time relist Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia struck out: The court denied without comment the petition brought by Roberto Clemente’s family over Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image, which raised questions about takings of intangible property and Puerto Rico’s sovereign immunity.

After a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 new relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week. Several come in pairs or trios, and the federal government – the court’s most successful repeat litigant – advocates review in three of them.

The government seeks asylum – from the D.C. Circuit

The most consequential new relist this week may be Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. On his first day back in office, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10888, which suspended the entry of aliens “engaged in the invasion across the southern border” and barred those who violate the suspension from invoking provisions of the immigration laws that would let them stay, including asylum.

Three nonprofits and 13 individuals sued. The district court certified a class of people subject to the proclamation who are or will be present in the United States. It held unlawful the proclamation’s restrictions on asylum and other statutory protections, as well as its authorization of removal procedures outside those established by Congress, and issued a classwide injunction. A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit narrowed the class definition, but affirmed. It reasoned that although asylum is discretionary, the executive cannot categorically deny covered migrants access to asylum by proclamation and informal guidance rather than through the procedures Congress prescribed. Judge Justin Walker dissented in relevant part.

The solicitor general’s petition argues that asylum is discretionary and that the president may categorically deny it to those covered by the proclamation. Requiring the government to accept applications it has already decided to reject, the government contends, serves no purpose. It also challenges the classwide injunction and the breadth of the certified class. The government argues that the ruling threatens to revive chaos at the border. Iowa and 21 other states support the petition, arguing that the decision undermines the federal duty to protect the states against invasion.

The respondents’ brief in opposition argues that Congress expressly gave noncitizens physically present in the United States the right to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered, and that the president cannot eliminate that right by proclamation. They emphasize the absence of a circuit split and dispute the government’s claims that the policy was responsible for reducing border crossings. They call the remedial issues fact-bound and say the government overstates the border crisis, noting that apprehensions had already fallen more than 90% from their peak before the proclamation.

The D.C. Circuit’s mandate is stayed, leaving the asylum restrictions in place for now. The absence of a split weighs against review, but the invalidation of a major administration policy could well persuade the justices to take another trip to the border. Will the court resolve this case quickly or let it sit for a while as it decides what to do, as it has in other high-profile cases?

Our first group of cases asks whether Washington may regulate private companies that run federal immigration detention centers. In GEO Group, Inc. v. Nwauzor, a class of detainees and the state sued GEO, which operates the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma under a federal contract, for not paying Washington’s minimum wage to detainees in a voluntary work program for which ICE reimburses $1 a day. GEO argues it’s not a conventional labor relationship, but just an effort to prevent the detainees from becoming restless from idleness. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit certified the question to the Washington Supreme Court, which held that the state minimum-wage law applied to the detained workers. A divided panel of the 9th Circuit then rejected GEO’s supremacy clause defenses, leaving GEO with a judgment it puts at about $37 million. Seven judges voted to rehear the case en banc, and six joined dissents, arguing that (among other things) the state law “interferes with federal immigration-detention policy” and thus directly regulates the federal government.

GEO argues that Washington cannot regulate a federal detention program through a contractor while exempting its own detainees from the wage law. Washington and the detainees respond that the law applies equally to every private detention contractor, whether it works for a city, the state or the federal government, and that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit applies the same test as the 9th. The detainees also note that ICE has since revised its detention standards, which they say limits the decision’s future impact.

In a court-invited amicus brief, the U.S. solicitor general recommends granting review. The government argues that the law discriminates against the federal government, because Washington exempts its own facilities while barring itself from contracting with private ones, and that federal statutes leave detainee pay to the Secretary of Homeland Security. It also says the decision conflicts with a decision of the 3rd Circuit ruling on a New Jersey law targeting private detention contractors.

GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson challenges a 2023 Washington statute regulating private civil detention facilities, which GEO says reaches its Tacoma facility alone. The district court preliminarily enjoined it, but the 9th Circuit vacated that ruling, rejecting GEO’s direct regulation and preemption claims and remanding on its discrimination claim against private contractors. GEO says Washington is micromanaging federal detention by regulating a contractor; the state says its requirements resemble those governing other civil facilities. It also points to further proceedings on remand as a reason not to intervene yet.

A grant in Nwauzor seems likely; Ferguson presents a closer question, but at minimum it seems likely to be held if Nwauzor is granted.

Two companies that went public while business was booming present a question of required disclosures in federal securities filings: How much bad news must a company reveal? Two related relists ask the justices to clarify when withholding information makes an IPO registration statement misleading under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933.

In Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, the online brokerage rode the GameStop meme-stock frenzy and Dogecoin boom into its July 2021 IPO. Robinhood warned that trading might decline and provided an estimate of second-quarter revenue, but investors say it withheld information showing that trading and other business metrics were already declining. A district court dismissed their claims, but a divided panel of the 9th Circuit revived them. Robinhood’s petition argues that merely omitting material information cannot create liability unless the omission makes an affirmative statement misleading or violates a specific disclosure requirement. The investors respond that the company’s disclosures presented a misleading picture of its performance. The U.S. solicitor general, invited to weigh in, recommends granting review on the Section 11 misleading-omissions question, but not on a separate question concerning disclosures of known trends under Item 303 of Regulation S-K (which the agency is reviewing).

In ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, a webinar-platform provider prospered as businesses moved online during the pandemic. Investors allege that the company knew before the IPO that many pandemic-era customers did not intend to renew. An unpublished 9th Circuit memorandum revived the suit. ON24 asks whether describing an unmaterialized risk as hypothetical is misleading, alleging a split with the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd and 10th Circuits, and raises two questions that overlap with Robinhood’s. ON24 argues that the court improperly required it to predict future customer cancellations; the investors respond that “the warned-of risk was already materializing.” ON24 also asks the justices either to grant its petition or hold it for Robinhood. Leadersel Innotech answers that the 9th Circuit decision is non-precedential and that the panel found the risk had already begun to materialize.

With the solicitor general supporting review in Robinhood, a grant there looks plausible. Whether ON24 gets invited along is less certain. It seems a likelier hold.

It’s not every week that the Taliban is a respondent in the Supreme Court. That said, it has not responded, leaving an Afghan diplomat filing an amicus brief to oppose review – not on the Taliban’s behalf, but on behalf of the Afghan people.

When the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, the Treasury Department blocked billions of dollars that Da Afghanistan Bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Victims holding judgments against the Taliban sought to execute on the funds under Section 201(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which makes the blocked assets of a terrorist party and its “agency or instrumentality” subject to execution.

A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit affirmed the denial of turnover. It held that an entity’s status as a terrorist organization’s instrumentality must be determined when its assets were blocked, before the Taliban installed its officials at the bank. Separately, the panel rejected other plaintiffs’ attempt at prejudgment attachment, holding that Da Afghanistan Bank enjoys sovereign immunity as the central bank of Afghanistan, which the executive continues to recognize as a foreign state. Judge Richard Sullivan dissented.

In Havlish v. The Taliban, judgment holders challenge the blocking-date rule, alleging a conflict between the 2nd Circuit and the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 9th and 11th Circuits. They are backed by Iowa and 30 other states.

In Owens v. The Taliban, plaintiffs who lacked judgments when the district court ruled say the 2nd Circuit is the first court of appeals to require courts to defer to the executive on “foreign state” status, and thus “breaks with th[e] consensus” positions of the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd, and 6th Circuits. Ashton v. The Taliban joins Owens in arguing that courts should not defer to the executive branch in determining whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, and seeks a GVR in light of this year’s decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A.

As noted, no respondent has appeared. The only opposition is an amicus brief jointly filed in the three cases by Naseer Faiq, chargé d’affaires of Afghanistan’s mission to the United Nations, who says no one is currently authorized to appear for Afghanistan in U.S. courts. He argues that the facts are unlikely to recur, that there is no circuit split, and that the immunity issue affects only the petitioners’ priority among creditors. The Havlish petitioners have sought leave to respond, arguing that the legal question is likely to recur in terrorism litigation and does indeed implicate a circuit split.

At the very least, the court will need more time to figure out what to do when the respondent seems unwilling to appear to defend the cases.

How many places can a state declare off-limits to firearms before the Second Amendment right to carry in public becomes largely theoretical? That’s the question in Novotny v. Moore, a challenge to Maryland’s extensive restrictions on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”

Maryland prohibits licensed gun owners from carrying firearms in numerous locations, including public transportation, parks and forests, healthcare facilities, museums, stadiums, casinos, public demonstrations, and establishments serving alcohol. I thought this was America! A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld those restrictions, finding historical support for them under the Supreme Court’s decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Judge G. Steven Agee dissented as to many of the restrictions, warning that the majority had stretched the sensitive-places exception too far. The panel separately struck down Maryland’s presumptive ban on carrying firearms on private property open to the public.(After this year’s decision in Wolford v. Lopez, which struck down Hawaii’s similar private-property rule, Maryland dropped its own cert petition seeking review of that ruling.)

The gun owners’ petition argues that historical restrictions on carrying firearms in sensitive places were generally limited to locations where the government provides security, not ordinary places where people gather. Maryland responds that historical regulations support restrictions at crowded places and locations serving vulnerable populations, and contends that review is unnecessary because the lower courts largely agree on the governing principles.

Invoking Wolford, the petitioners ask the justices to grant review or at least send the case back for reconsideration. Whether the court is ready to take on the sensitive-places doctrine so soon after Wolford remains to be seen. But reconsideration under Wolford seems like a real possibility.

In Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, the Commission fined Sprint $12.2 million and T-Mobile $80.1 million for failing to adequately safeguard customers’ location information shared with third-party aggregators, including by continuing to disclose the information after learning of significant security vulnerabilities. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the penalties, concluding that information about a cellphone’s location – even when no call is underway – qualifies as confidential “customer proprietary network information” under the Communications Act.

The carriers’ petition argues that the statute protects only call-location information, not all device-location data. They also contend that the FCC circumvented a statutory penalty cap by treating separate relationships with third-party companies as multiple “continuing violations,” and that the D.C. Circuit improperly deferred to the agency’s interpretation despite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. But the carriers’ principal request is narrower: They ask the justices to send the case back in light of this year’s decision in FCC v. AT&T, which held that an FCC forfeiture order does not itself compel payment. That opinion, the carriers say, rested on a key government concession: A company can refuse to pay and contest the penalty in a subsequent enforcement proceeding with a jury. Sprint and T-Mobile say they paid under protest because the FCC’s orders demanded payment and existing precedent left them little choice. The government responds that the carriers always had the option not to pay, that they failed to preserve their claim of being misled, and that AT&T provides no reason for reconsideration. The carriers disagree.

A remand remains possible, although the government notes that the court rejected a comparable request from Verizon. For now, Sprint and T-Mobile are hoping the justices will take their call.

How long can a “hot pursuit” stay hot after police lose sight of the suspect? That’s the question in City of North Las Vegas v. Jones, a case arising from a search for a suspected domestic abuser that ended with police entering a stranger’s backyard and shooting two dogs. The suspect was never found.

After officers saw a man flee over a backyard wall, the officers stated that they established a neighborhood perimeter rather than pursuing him on foot. A K-9 officer arrived about 18 minutes later, and during the ensuing search, his police dog alerted them toward a walled backyard. An officer climbed in without a warrant. Three pit bulls emerged, two of which attacked the police dog and were shot. The dogs’ owners, Genoa Jones and Cornell Tinsley, sued. The district court granted the officers qualified immunity, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed on the warrantless-entry claim, holding that the officers had not been in immediate and continuous pursuit and that circuit precedent clearly established the search’s illegality. It left intact qualified immunity for shooting the dogs. Eight judges dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc.

The city’s petition argues that the officers never abandoned the pursuit: They say they established a perimeter and used a police dog to locate a potentially dangerous suspect. Even if the search was unlawful, the city argues, no sufficiently specific precedent clearly established that fact. It also asks the justices to hold that only Supreme Court decisions – not lower-court precedent – can clearly establish law for qualified-immunity purposes. The homeowners respond that the officers never actually established a perimeter or chased the suspect and instead just conducted a neighborhood-wide search without knowing his whereabouts.

The eight dissenting judges may help keep the petition warm. But the court closely reviews many petitions in cases where police are denied qualified immunity, and unless the error was clear enough to warrant summary reversal, the justices may let this pursuit go cold – perhaps with a dissent from denial of cert.

The court has enough to chew on that it seems likely to take a while to finish processing this week’s new offerings. As for me, I’ll be watching Monday’s orders to find out how much of this I get to reuse.

Issue: Whether the supremacy clause allows a state to reclassify federal immigration detainees participating in a federal work program as employees and thereby impose its state minimum-wage law just because a private contractor provides detention services at the federal facility where the detainees are housed.

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by failing to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider material, without an inquiry into whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading; and (2) whether an issuer violates Item 303 – and thus Section 11(a)’s required-statements prong – by failing to disclose and quantify interim financial data before quarterly reporting deadlines.

Issue: Whether Maryland’s numerous prohibitions on carrying firearms in many places frequented by the general public violate the Second and 14th Amendments.

City of North Las Vegas, Nevada v. Jones, 25-1355

Issues: (1) Whether officers’ warrantless search of a backyard in close proximity to the domestic violence victim’s residence was a lawful “hot pursuit” when the suspect’s trail was temporarily lost within the perimeter for approximately 18 minutes but recovered through immediate and continuous police efforts; (2) whether, even if the search did not qualify as a “hot pursuit,” the officers were entitled to qualified immunity because no “clearly established law” was violated; and (3) whether, in the interest of avoiding the perpetual flood of federal court qualified immunity litigation, the court should decide that clearly established law means only the decisions of the Supreme Court, and not lower court decisions, which fail to provide police departments with meaningful guidance because they are highly fact-determinative and subject to numerous differing and often contradictory judicial interpretations.

ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, 25-1376

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by describing unmaterialized risks as hypothetical; (2) whether an issuer violates Section 11(a)’s misleading-omissions prong whenever it omits information related to a disclosed fact regardless of whether the omission renders an affirmative statement misleading; and (3) whether an issuer violates Item 303 of Regulation S-K – and thus the prong of Section 11(a) prohibiting the omission of required statements – by failing to disclose immaterial facts as “known trends or uncertainties” that are reasonably likely to have a material impact on financial results.

Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, 25-1422

Issues: (1) Whether this court should grant, vacate, and remand in light of FCC v. AT&T, Inc. and the government’s concessions in that case; (2) whether “location” customer proprietary network information under 47 U.S.C. § 222 refers only to call-location information, not other formation about the location of a mobile device; and (3) whether the number of “continuing violations” arising from a single failure to act under 47 U.S.C. § 503(b) is a legal question for courts to decide, without deferring to the Federal Communications Commission’s conclusion.

Issue: Whether the supremacy clause permits a state to enact a law micromanaging the details of how a federal contractor must provide services at a federal detention facility, while exempting the state’s own detention facilities from all those requirements.

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, 26-239

Issues: (1) Whether Presidential Proclamation No. 10888 and its implementing guidance – which suspended the entry of certain aliens and precluded their access to statutory provisions that would enable their continued presence in the country, including asylum – are lawful; (2) whether 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1) bars the classwide relief entered by the district court; and (3) whether the class definition comports with Article III and Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

Issue: Whether, under the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, a plaintiff’s right to execute on blocked assets depends on whether the assets’ owner was a terrorist party or its agency or instrumentality at the time the assets were blocked.

Issue: Whether, in light of the court’s intervening decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A., which confirms that a court – not the Executive Branch – must resolve through ordinary statutory construction whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, the judgment below should be vacated and remanded so that the Second Circuit must reconsider, under the correct framework, whether the Taliban and its instrumentalities are entitled to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act.

Issue: Whether the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act requires courts to independently interpret its provisions, or whether a court must defer to State Department websites and Department of Justice litigation filings in determining whether an entity is entitled to sovereign immunity under the FSIA.

Issue: Whether private instruction in courses required for state licensure constitutes a government speech.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether, in a use-of-force case which involves multiple instances of force, Barnes v. Felix requires that each use-of-force be analyzed progressively from before the first instance of force used through the last instance of force used, considering the information known to the officer, the suspect’s prior actions (including any compliance, non-compliance, resistance, and reaching or grabbing for a weapon), and the suspect’s reactions to those prior use(s)-of-force; and (2) whether, when analyzing a defendant law enforcement officer’s motion brought under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), in a use-of-force case where body camera video clearly depicts the entire lead-up to and application of force by a law enforcement officer, whether the lower courts may analyze the clearly established prong of qualified immunity at a more general, plaintiff-friendly, level than at the motion for summary judgment stage of litigation.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a violation of a clearly established constitutional right; and (2) whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a complete lack of training on the constitutional right in question.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issue: Whether the principles of Hope v. Pelzer are limited to Eighth Amendment claims or extend to free speech and free exercise clause claims such that petitioner’s constitutional claims should not be barred by qualified immunity.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

StandWithUs Center for Legal Justice v. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 25-1404

Issues: (1) Whether the harassers’ subjective discriminatory intent is an element of a hostile environment claim under Title VI; and (2) whether the First Amendment bars a plaintiff from pleading a Title VI hostile environment claim based on “protected speech.”

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issue: Whether the law clearly established that the officer’s use of a less-lethal projectile, under the totality of the circumstances, constituted an unreasonable use of force in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

(Relisted after the Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issue: Whether an automobile is per se an instrumentality of interstate commerce, which would make a federal offense of every kidnapping involving an automobile under 18 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1).

(Relisted after the Oct. 16 and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues:(1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

(Relisted after the Oct. 16 and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

(Relisted after the Oct. 16 and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

(Relisted after the Oct. 16 and Nov. 6 conferences.)

John P. Elwood is a partner at Arnold & Porter in Washington, D.C., specializing in appellate litigation and administrative law.

#7785. California coalitions sue to block Gov. Newsom’s commutation of over 500 death row sentences

California Gov. Gavin Newsom looks on during a bill-signing event Aug. 21, 2025, in Sacramento, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

District attorneys and victims’ families have taken their fight to the California Supreme Court over California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute over 500 death row penalty sentences.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which represents the plaintiffs, argued Monday that the governor was required to give formal notice to district attorneys before commuting 548 death penalty sentences. The plaintiffs also challenged Newsom’s broad death penalty commutations without considering individual circumstances, beyond whether a person has more than one felony conviction. Existing law permits crime victims the opportunity to speak before a governor can commute someone.

“Gov. Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law,” the plaintiffs said. “He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand,” according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 the commutations of all people on death row to life in prison without parole. The governor wrote a letter that said state-sanctioned killing undermines the legal system’s foundation and counters California’s values.

Newsom, who has served two terms, declared a moratorium on all executions in 2019 and leaves office in January.

#7784. Federal judge sides with Biden Labor Dept. on ESG fiduciary rule

A Texas Northern District Court judge said the rule is still valid under Loper Bright and does not violate the Employment Retirement Income Security Act of 1974.

The Labor Department rule in question, “Prudence and Loyalty in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights,” was finalized in 2022 and has been in effect since January 2023. The rule was designed to overturn guidance the agency issued in 2020 under the first Trump administration that forbade fiduciaries from utilizing “non-pecuniary” factors in investment decisions.

The 2022 rule was designed to overturn a “chilling effect” that the Biden administration’s Labor Department said was witnessed under the 2020 rule. The guidance revised the agency’s tiebreaker standard to allow for consideration of collateral benefits like ESG in the event that two or more investments would equally serve the plan’s best interests but it would be imprudent to invest in both or all options.

The DOL rule has been repeatedly challenged by a coalition of 26 Republican-led states, who argued it runs afoul of ERISA and exceeded the agency’s statutory authority. However, Kacsmaryk disagreed in his Feb. 14 ruling and said such a reading of the law “embodies the wooden textualism that courts should endeavor to avoid.”

“Under the rule, a fiduciary faced with choosing between investment options — that all equally serve the beneficiaries' financial interests — does not advance the interests of nonbeneficiaries nor act for a purpose other than their financial benefit when he chooses based on collateral factors,” the judge ruled. “Plaintiffs' interpretation of ERISA would demand arbitrary randomness to choose between such investment options.”

The Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo case — which determined the fate of the Chevron doctrine — was decided in the time between Kacsmaryk’s initial dismissal of the case and when the plaintiffs and the Biden administration’s Labor Department argued before the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court’s decision in June 2024 overturned the Chevron doctrine, which previously directed courts to give agencies deference in their interpretations of ambiguous law statutes.

While the parties had opposing views on how Chevron’s demise affected the case at hand, the Fifth Circuit refused to rule on the case, but vacated the initial dismissal and asked Kacsmaryk whether the rule can be squared with ERISA or the Administrative Procedure Act in light of Loper Bright.

Kacsmaryk said Loper Bright “did not disturb how courts evaluate a rule under the APA's arbitrary and capricious standard,” in his ruling Friday. He said the overturn of the Chevron doctrine should change how courts should interpret statutes, but not how they review the reasonableness of agency decisions.

The judge said that the tiebreaker standard in the 2022 rule does not violate ERISA’s duty of loyalty nor its requirement that fiduciaries act “solely” and for the “exclusive” benefit of the plan’s financial interests. Kacsmaryk said ERISA defines “whose interest the fiduciary must protect” and what their purpose is, but “says nothing of what they may consider.”

“Just as a driver, duty-bound to choose the fastest route to his destination, may choose the most scenic of two routes that each bring him to his destination at the same time, so too can a fiduciary choose a preferable investment option between two that will equally satisfy his duty of loyalty,” the judge wrote.

The coalition of Republican-led states were also joined in their lawsuit by public oilfield services company Liberty Energy, where Energy Secretary Chris Wright served as CEO at the time. The plaintiffs have previously signaled a willingness to fight the case all the way to the Supreme Court, but first it will return to the Fifth Circuit panel that initially heard the arguments.

However, it remains to be seen how the Trump administration’s Labor Department will handle the case. Experts have previously expressed concerns about the DOL’s rule being one of the Biden administration’s ESG-related regulations likely to be put on the chopping block under Trump.

#7782. The New FBI: Better Technology to Meet the Mission

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by FBI Director Kash Patel was published by Nextgov/FCW on November 10, 2026.

Of this FBI’s many historic successes over the last 21 months of the Trump administration, perhaps our most consequential has been our complete overhaul in technology capabilities. For too long, outdated technology and bureaucratic processes slowed the Bureau's ability to deliver results. Those days are over.

Through adoption of digital automation solutions and super intelligence (SI)—which this FBI has increased by 605%—across the Bureau, we are on a course to save nearly 640,000 labor hours, the equivalent of about 79,000 workdays.

Our SI program began by listening to the people doing the work. Through our SI Champions Program and Task Force, we started collecting success stories from across the field, and early results have been tremendous. In the past 90 days alone, users of our programs report saving an estimated 829 hours, about 104 workdays, by automating transcription, accelerating translation, reducing data triage, and streamlining jail call review. If that pace holds, every year these use cases alone will return more than 3,300 hours, or over 413 workdays.

These are much bigger than numbers—they are cases that matter to the American people. For example, in San Antonio, during multiple investigations of human trafficking, drug trafficking, fraud, and money laundering, one wiretap alone produced more than 1,900 sessions of poor-quality audio. SI transcription saved roughly 633 hours of manual work.

More importantly, in one specific case, the time saved allowed agents to move quickly enough to help rescue a trafficking victim and return the victim safely to their family. In another case out of Mobile, analysis of jail calls in threat cases used to take months. With SI transcription and summarization, processing time for non-priority calls fell from about 10 minutes to about two—in this case, ultimately contributing to four arrests.

Our digital automation solutions program uses software bots to handle repetitive, transaction-based computer tasks, freeing people for analytical work that requires human judgment. Twenty-nine offices across the Bureau have deployed automations.

As of October, we have fielded more than 121 of them, connected to dozens of existing FBI applications, saving over 635,000 labor hours. One specific automation helps our Human Resources Division enter benefits data for new employees, saving about 1,275 hours a year and giving new hires a more efficient transition.

Hippo Chat, the FBI’s new SI chatbot built directly into our systems, reduces administrative workload associated with file reviews and other evaluations. It synthesizes large quantities of documents, like large search warrant returns, into a readable format with the relevant information—reviewing thousands of photos at one time, organizing them into a spreadsheet for easy triage by cases agents and analysts and more.

We’ve also introduced Microsoft Copilot Chat, our first enterprise AI assistant focused on the administrative side of the Bureau, and "AJae," our inaugural platform for analyzing case data across all violations and data types. These apps free up thousands of critical hours per year for our agents and intelligence analysts in the field. None of this would be possible without our private sector partners and their cutting-edge integration to advance our mission capabilities—marking the most wide-ranging and impactful partnerships for technology in Bureau history.

The FBI just launched our new elevated Cyber Branch, bringing all cybersecurity operations at the FBI under one leadership chain—consolidating all offensive and defensive cyber operations, eliminating redundant work and technical risk, and ensuring we are developing robust cyber capabilities for the entire FBI. We’re evolving how we do business to better meet the demands of the dynamic threat landscape and provide better resources for the agents, analysts, and professional staff working hard in the field. This will greatly accelerate our work to ensure the FBI maintains the strongest cyber infrastructure in the world.

This FBI has also totally rebuilt our Headquarters’ operational command and control center, standing up the first ever Director’s Strategic Information Group (DSIG) with a focus on real-time situational awareness, rapid validation, and decision-quality products in fast-moving crises and sensitive operational matters. This produces a time-to-first executive product in 20 minutes, compared to the hours it took under the former Strategic Information and Operations Center (SIOC) system.

This is the technology that has strongly contributed to the most prolific reduction in violent crime in American history: 71,650 violent crime arrests, a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration; 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs seized, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans; 5,801 child victims identified or located, up 25%; 6,744 arrests tied to foreign terrorist organizations, an increase of 1,057%; 10 fugitives from the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list arrested, including alleged murderers, rapists, and other violent criminals—2.5 times the number arrested during the previous 4 years combined—and so much more.

The principle is simple: Technology should serve the mission, allowing our people to better serve Americans. Every hour we return to our workforce is an hour for the work only they can do: crushing violent crime, defending the homeland, protecting victims, and stopping threats before they reach our communities. Mission First.

Kash Patel is the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

#7780. Justices see immigration contract dispute as raising the possibility of major limits on administrative power

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards showed a court open to the possibility of a major limitation on the ability of agencies to impose fines or penalties under internal adjudicative processes, at least without ready review in court.

The constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article II of the Constitution). The Supreme Court always has recognized that it is permissible for officials in the executive branch – who don’t have the protections (including life tenure) that Article III gives to federal judges – to resolve questions in a proceeding that looks an awful lot like the kind of trial you might see in a federal court. And it also on several occasions has invalidated schemes that seemed to the court to go too far in that direction. To pick the most famous example, the justices invalidated the initial version of the Bankruptcy Code of 1978 because it gave undue adjudicative responsibility to bankruptcy “judges” that are not protected by Article III. What the court has never done well is explain exactly how far such powers can go. Nevertheless, recent decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a great willingness to rein in the powers traditionally granted to the administrative state.

This case presents a dispute as to whether employers under the H-2A visa program (for temporary foreign agricultural workers) gave those employees certain things they were promised before being admitted to the United States. Conventionally, when the Department of Labor decided that an employer had failed to treat workers as it promised pre-admission, it imposed fines or penalties in an administrative proceeding, often handing the funds over to the employees as compensation in the nature of back pay. The question for the justices is whether Article III of the Constitution can tolerate that dispute being resolved internally by DOL employees rather than by judges in a federal court.

The government sees the dispute as squarely involving two categories of so-called “public rights” for which Article I treatment is permitted: the immigration power and public benefits. The immigration power is involved because the workers were permitted to enter the country on the condition that the employer treat them as agreed; the public benefit power is involved because the right to enter is a benefit almost entirely within the discretion of the executive.

Several of the justices found that argument rather weak. Chief Justice John Roberts, for example, commented early on that the leading case about the immigration power (Oceanic Steam Navigation v Mellor) “had to do very much with entry, a condition of entry, and loathsome diseases. This strikes me as significantly different. … You’re trying to leverage an entry several weeks, months … in the past to the particular condition of work that doesn’t seem to have much to do with the actual entry.” For the chief justice, the government was trying to “leverage what is a significant barrier to entry, where you have a lot of deference to the executive branch,” and “trying to … extend that broad authority beyond the justification for its application.” He repeatedly emphasized that the specifics of the case “look more like a condition of employment rather than … entry.”

In a similar vein, Justice Amy Coney Barrett stated to Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris (arguing for the government): “I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our immigration tradition without an Article III court. But the fines, I’m wondering if they’re different. …. So I’m … wondering here why that wouldn’t be the case for the alien. If the alien violated some sort of condition on the H-2A visa, why wouldn’t the alien be entitled to an Article III court before the alien had to pay that kind of a fine?” At which point Justice Neil Gorsuch chimed in that he “thought [an earlier case had said that] confiscating property goes to an Article III court when you’re trying to confiscate property from aliens. … I thought we decided a long time ago that you’ve got to go to an Article III court. Are … you resisting that?”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh pointed to yet another precedent on civil penalties: “In Tull [v. United States], we said … and this is 40 years ago – a civil penalty was a type of remedy at common law that could only be enforced in courts of law. …. That’s a fairly definitive statement in our precedent. What … are we supposed to do with that?”

That’s not to say that all of the justices sided against the government. Justice Elena Kagan, for example, found the case well within the boundaries of existing doctrine. To Harris, she commented early on: “[I]sn’t there a condition of entry here? … [T]hey wouldn’t be admitted unless the employer had promised certain things.” To Robert Johnson arguing on behalf of the employer – a different Robert Johnson, not the blues singer – she was much more pointed:

Offering a parallel perspective, Ketanji Brown Jackson emphasized that the court in numerous contexts has approved administrative adjudication of civil penalties. She repeatedly challenged Johnson to reconcile his argument with those decisions.

But ominous for the government was some repeated questioning of Harris about “the best way for you to lose” (as Justice Sonia Sotomayor put it). From early on in the argument, even the justices who seem most likely to accept the constitutionality of the arrangement were trying to help Harris identify the least damaging way for the court to rule against her. At the beginning of her argument and throughout it, Harris emphasized to the justices that a broad ruling against her on the constitutional question would unsettle programs in a wide variety of areas, ranging from Medicare, to government contracts, to student loans, but that did not seem to make any headway for her.

It is not at all clear from the argument how exactly the justices are going to come down. Clearly a significant group are considering the idea that an award of civil penalties is too far removed from the entry of the employee to be protected by the “public rights” doctrine that would protect administrative determination of the right to enter. My guess is that even those justices don’t yet know how far they would be willing to go – or how far they can go and secure five votes of agreement. I expect this case to come down late and be sharply divided.

Correction (Nov. 15 at 6:12 p.m.): An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that “the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch” is in “Article I of the Constitution.”

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

#7779. Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

“North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”

“The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”

“By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

“North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”

Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance

Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.
